summary: This workflow builds a savings report by joining claims, benchmark, and case data, calculating a running savings total per member, parsing a note field, running a custom Python calculation, and producing a program-level summary through a separate macro. It scores 9/10, the highest difficulty band, mainly because of the Python tool [13] (no SQL equivalent) and the Macro [16] (logic lives in a separate file that must be migrated independently). RegEx [3] and Multi-Row Formula [12] add further rework because their logic needs different techniques in Redshift. Four separate output files also mean four separate SQL outputs to build and validate.

key_components.description: Loads claims, benchmarks, and case files, cleans/converts amount fields, parses a note field, and joins the three sources to calculate an 'allowed' and 'savings' amount.
Sorts records by member and service date, then calculates a running savings total per member row by row.
Runs Python code that flags claims as 'top saver' if their savings amount is above the 90th percentile.
Summarizes savings by program using a separate macro file, combined with totals from a Summarize tool [17].
Writes four separate outputs: unmatched claims, claim savings (CSV and database file), and program summary.

risks.title: Python logic has no SQL equivalent
risks.detail: The Python tool [13] computes a 'top saver' flag using a statistical percentile (quantile). Redshift has no Python UDF support after June 2026, so this logic must be rewritten in SQL (e.g. using PERCENTILE_CONT) or run outside Redshift.

risks.title: Macro logic not visible in this file
risks.detail: The Macro [16] calls a separate file (wf4_program_summary.yxmc) whose internal logic is not included in these facts. It must be assessed and migrated on its own before the full workflow's difficulty is known.

risks.title: Running total needs a window function with explicit frame
risks.detail: The Multi-Row Formula [12] builds a running total row-by-row, which translates to a SQL window function (SUM OVER). Redshift requires an explicit frame clause (e.g. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) when ORDER BY is used, or results will differ.

risks.title: Unmatched join records used downstream
risks.detail: The Join [6] passes its unmatched (non-joining) records to a separate output. This must be rebuilt as a distinct LEFT JOIN ... WHERE ... IS NULL query, since Redshift doesn't have a built-in 'unmatched' output like Alteryx.

risks.title: RegEx behavior differs between Alteryx and Redshift
risks.detail: The RegEx tool [3] is case-insensitive and extracts a capture group, but Redshift's REGEXP_SUBSTR is case-sensitive by default and returns the whole match unless extra parameters ('i', 'e') are added. Redshift also defaults to POSIX regex syntax, not Perl-style, so the pattern may need rewriting.

risks.title: Currency text-to-number conversion is fragile
risks.detail: Formulas [2] and [8] strip currency symbols and commas before converting text to numbers. In Redshift, any value that doesn't match the expected format will fail the entire query rather than just that row, so all formats in the real data must be accounted for.

next_steps: Obtain and analyze the macro file wf4_program_summary.yxmc separately before finalizing the migration plan.
Decide how to replace the Python top-saver logic [13], e.g. rewrite with a SQL percentile function or run it in an external process.
Rebuild the running savings calculation [12] as a SQL window function with an explicit frame clause.
Test the regex pattern from [3] in Redshift with the 'i' and 'e' parameters, and confirm POSIX vs Perl syntax compatibility.
Recreate the unmatched-join output [6] as a separate LEFT JOIN query with an IS NULL filter.
Audit the real claims data for all currency formatting variants to ensure the CAST/REPLACE logic in [2] and [8] won't fail on real values.
